narrative: The model estimated a 57.6% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, it found failure slightly more likely than passing, and because law school admission here is tied to that risk, your application was rejected. The decision was not driven by your gender or race. The strongest concern was your Year 3 class standing: you were in the second decile, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile. This low relative ranking pushed the prediction most strongly toward failure. Your LSAT score of 35.5 was the second most influential factor, and it actually worked in your favor by lowering the estimated failure risk. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.50, above the accepted average of 3.23, was the third most influential factor and also reduced the risk. Even so, those positives were not enough to outweigh the Year 3 academic-standing concern. Next, ask admissions for a review or conditional pathway, speak with an academic advisor about why your Year 3 rank fell, and build a concrete bar-preparation and academic-improvement plan. If allowed, provide updated evidence of readiness and ask what threshold would support reconsideration.
